Rams history is so weird to me, why'd they ever leave LA? Were they not popular there? That was before I was into the NFL

When they moved to L.A. from Cleveland (having won the 1945 NFL title their last year in Cleveland behind a controversial play), they became the first major pro sports team to play games on the west coast. Part of their first agreement with the L.A. Coliseum included a clause that they have at least one black player, so for their first year in L.A. in 1946, they signed Kenny Washington, a UCLA star who had roomed with Jackie Robinson while with the Bruins, and the Rams thus became the first team to integrate. In 1948, Ram horns were painted on the sides of the helmet, making them also the first team to display a logo on their helmets. Throughout the 1950's, they became the first team to use three wide receivers in their principal offense, and displayed one of the most prolific offenses in NFL history. The record for passing yards in one game, even with today's pass-happy league, is STILL owned by 1951 QB Norm Van Brocklin, with 554 yards. It is one of the older records in league history. These teams were wildly popular. Despite the arrival of the Dodgers from Brooklyn in 1958, the formation of the Angels in 1960, and the arrival of basketball's Lakers from Minnesota in 1960, the Rams regularly drew 85,000 to 93,000 per game, though in the late fifties and early sixties the Rams weren't as good on the field as their attendance numbers were off it.

In the late 1960's, the "Fearsome Foursome" became the NFL's first truly dominant defensive front four, and the Rams began a period of sustained success. From 1967-1980, the Rams won their division 9 times, including six straight from 1973-79. For four straight years they lost the NFC Championship, before finally winning it in 1979 before losing the Super Bowl to the Steelers 31-19, in a game that was much closer than the scoreline. The biggest problem they faced off the field was the NFL's blackout rule, which forbade teams from local television if their games did not sell out. The L.A. Coliseum's 93,000+ seating capacity made that difficult, and so in 1980, the team moved to Aneheim and began a long string of sellouts at the 69,000 capacity stadium. Also in 1980, owner Carroll Rosenbloom died in a drowning accident, and his wife Georgia Frontiere, assumed 70% control of the team. She promptly fired her own stepson from management, and set about running the franchise into the ground.

In 1982, the Raiders moved down south from Oakland, and the result was that the Rams fanbase was split in two. This was also at about the same time as the age of their roster caught up with them, and they missed the playoffs for the first time in nearly a decade. In 1983, they drafted Eric Dickerson, and for a while, fortunes changed, with playoff runs peaking with NFC Championship Game appearances in 1985 and 1990. However, The firing of legendary USC coach John Robinson in 1991 sowed the seeds that would cause the team to move.

With attendance slowly decreasing, what the Rams did not need was a stagnant offense, and losing records- two things Chuck Knox brought to the team from 1992-1994, the Rams last year in L.A.. The blackout rule reared its ugly head again, and the Rams suffered even further. Orange County, CA was a major defense industry hub, and with massive layoffs due to the end of The Cold War, the area was going through a significant economic downturn. Unable to secure funding for a new stadium, Georgia Frontiere, a former nightclub singer who had married four times before meeting Rosenbloom, began shopping the team around to prospective cities. Fans blamed her mismanagement for the teams troubles. She attempted to move the team to St. Louis, but the move was voted down 21-6 with 3 abstentions. The NFL cited 50 successful years in L.A. and said that 5 bad years could be corrected, but she then threatened legal action, and, eventually, the NFL- expressly because they did not want a long protracted legal battle at that particular time, reversed their decision and allowed the Rams to move to St. Louis for the 1995 season. Yet another in a decently sized list of franchises managed so poorly that they relocated. Some teams SHOULD move. Some teams didn't have much of a choice. The Rams were not one of those teams.
